title: The Sharpest Look Yet at the Tau's Tiny Magnet
hook: Every charged particle is a tiny magnet, and quantum jitters nudge its strength. Measuring that nudge tests the Standard Model — and CMS just made the best check yet for the tau lepton.
key_points: A particle's 'anomalous magnetic moment' (g−2) measures how quantum fluctuations shift its magnetism from the simplest prediction.
Any deviation from theory could betray unknown particles — the reason the muon's g−2 is watched so closely.
The tau's g−2 is barely constrained: the tau lives less than a trillionth of a second, too briefly to store in a ring.
CMS used 'ultraperipheral' lead-lead collisions, where two nuclei's photon clouds fuse (γγ→ττ) without the nuclei touching.
The result pins the tau's anomalous moment between −0.039 and 0.032 — the most precise LHC measurement yet, matching QED.
content_html: Spin a charged particle and it behaves like a tiny magnet. The exact strength of that magnet is predicted with extraordinary precision — and tiny quantum corrections from fleeting "virtual" particles shift it by a hair. Measuring that shift, called g−2, is one of physics' sharpest tests for undiscovered particles. CMS has now made the best such measurement for the tau, the heaviest cousin of the electron.
extra_html: The muon's g−2 grabs headlines because its measured value has flirted with disagreeing with theory. The tau's version is far less explored: the tau lives less than a trillionth of a second, far too briefly to store in a ring the way muons are. So CMS turned to "ultraperipheral" lead-lead collisions, where two lead nuclei skim past each other and their intense electromagnetic fields — clouds of photons — collide to make tau pairs (γγ→ττ) without the nuclei themselves touching. Fitting the taus' momenta across four decay channels, CMS constrained the tau's anomalous magnetic moment to between −0.039 and 0.032 at 95% confidence — the most precise result for this process at the LHC so far, and in agreement with quantum electrodynamics. Attribution: CMS Collaboration, arXiv (2026).

related.title: The Standard Model
related.hook: Almost everything around you is built from a handful of particles obeying three forces — and one theory predicts it all with jaw-dropping precision, yet still can't explain gravity.

related.title: How Many Elementary Particles Are There, Really?
related.hook: Count the Standard Model's particles and you might say 17 — but tweak the rules and the tally climbs past 900, with one rigorous answer that isn't even a whole number.

related.title: The Four Fundamental Forces
related.hook: Every push and pull in the universe — from falling apples to exploding stars — comes down to just four basic forces. Two you feel daily; two hide inside the atom.

flashcards.prompt: What does a particle's 'anomalous magnetic moment' (g−2) measure?
flashcards.back_html: How much quantum fluctuations — clouds of fleeting virtual particles — shift the particle's magnetism away from the simplest theoretical prediction.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the tau lepton's g−2 so much harder to measure than the muon's?

choices.text: The tau lives less than a trillionth of a second, too briefly to store in a ring
The tau carries no electric charge, so it feels no magnetic force
The tau is lighter than the electron, so its magnetism is tiny

flashcards.explanation_html: Muons can be stored in a ring and watched wobble; the tau decays far too fast for that, so CMS had to infer its moment from tau-pair production instead.

flashcards.prompt: How did CMS produce tau pairs without smashing the lead nuclei together?
flashcards.back_html: In "ultraperipheral" collisions the nuclei skim past each other and their photon clouds fuse (γγ→ττ) — the nuclei themselves never touch.

flashcards.prompt: Why do physicists care about measuring g−2 as precisely as possible?

choices.text: A deviation from the predicted value could reveal undiscovered particles
It sets the particle's electric charge

flashcards.explanation_html: Virtual copies of unknown particles would nudge g−2; a measured value off from theory is one of physics' sharpest hints that something new is hiding.
